source.note: The source is this repository's own Python implementation, not a second checkout. Cadenza is being rewritten in place (cadenza#8): `src/cadenza/` and `tests/` are the specification until a later PR retires them, so every inventory here is collected from the working tree at the recorded revision.

suite_baseline.reconciliation: `PYTHONPATH=src PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 python3 -m pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider` at a5672f8 on CPython 3.12.3: 330 passed. No module is skipped at collection time, so collected == the sum of the eight per-file inventories with nothing left over. See parity/source-inventory.manifest.json.

file.note: 9 test functions, 97 collected node ids. Five of the nine are parametrized over the modules the walk finds: four over all 20 Python modules and one over the 7 under `cadenza.domain`, which is 87 of the 97 by itself.

systematic_mappings.from: `@pytest.mark.parametrize("path", MODULES, ids=module_name)`, over the 20 Python modules `PACKAGE_ROOT.rglob("*.py")` finds
systematic_mappings.to: `parametrize(name, PER_MODULE, ...)` over the 18 TypeScript modules the walk over `src/` finds, with the repo-relative path as the id
systematic_mappings.why: This is the whole of why cadenza#8 re-points this file instead of transcribing it. The two module sets are not the same set with different spellings: 12 Python modules have a TypeScript counterpart, 8 are `__init__.py` package initialisers or `__about__.py` and have none, and 6 TypeScript modules exist that Python never had (`canonical-json`, `frozen`, and the four `python-*` standard-library ports, D-0018). So each of the four per-module functions contributes 12 `adapted` entries and 8 `waived` ones, and the 6 modules with no source case are declared `target_only_tests` rather than left unaccounted.
systematic_mappings.affects: 80 of the 97 cases: the four functions parametrized over all 20 modules

systematic_mappings.why: The id has to name the thing the case is about, and in this tree that is a file rather than a dotted module name. Paths are spelled with forward slashes on every platform, and the walk sorts them, so the ids are byte-stable across the ubuntu, macos and windows cells rather than depending on `readdirSync` order or the platform separator.

systematic_mappings.from: `imported_modules(path)`, an `ast.walk` collecting `ast.Import` and `ast.ImportFrom` with relative levels resolved
systematic_mappings.to: `importsIn(source, from)`, a `ts.createSourceFile` walk collecting import declarations, `export ... from` re-exports, `import(...)` calls, `require(...)` calls, `import x = require(...)`, and `import("...").X` type nodes, with relative specifiers resolved by path arithmetic
systematic_mappings.why: The source's docstring states the property that matters -- an import nested in a function or under `TYPE_CHECKING` is still an import, and importing the tree would not see either -- and TypeScript has strictly more routes with that property. A re-export has no Python counterpart at all and is how a layer leaks through a barrel, so the sweep covers it. Resolution is path arithmetic rather than a filesystem lookup, because the detector's own cases name modules that do not exist; `tsc` is what checks a specifier resolves, and this only has to agree about which file it resolves to.
systematic_mappings.affects: the 7 detector cases and all 87 per-module cases

systematic_mappings.to: `DOMAIN_ALLOWED_BUILTINS`, an allowlist naming both the module and the bindings it may contribute: `node:crypto` for `createHash`, `node:os` for `homedir`, `node:net` for `isIP`
systematic_mappings.why: A denylist is the wrong shape here for a reason specific to Node rather than to taste. `node:net` IS the socket module the source's denylist names first, and `isIP` is a pure predicate that happens to live in it, so a denylist either forbids `node:net` and fails on `src/domain/python-urlsplit.ts` today, or admits it and admits `createConnection` with it. Naming the bindings is what separates the two. The allowlist also fails closed, which the denylist does not: a `node:` module nobody thought of is a violation rather than an omission, and a namespace or default import of an allowed module is refused because neither can be checked binding by binding. Measured: a planted `import * as os from "node:os"` turns the case red, and so does `createConnection`.
systematic_mappings.affects: the 7 cases of 'the domain performs no I/O'

systematic_mappings.to: the normalised package name of a bare specifier, and the unscoped half of a scoped one, matched against `{"claude-org-runtime", "interlock"}`
systematic_mappings.why: The source's two spellings are Python module names, and the same two dependencies would arrive here written differently: `claude_org_runtime` becomes `claude-org-runtime` on a registry, and either could be scoped as `@suisya-systems/interlock`. Lower-casing and folding `_` to `-`, then checking the unscoped half as well, covers all of those without enumerating them. Measured: `@suisya-systems/interlock` and `claude-org-runtime/control-plane.js` both turn the case red.
systematic_mappings.affects: the 20 cases of 'no module imports interlock'

target_only_tests.why: Thirty-one, in two groups. Thirty are the six TypeScript modules that have no Python counterpart -- `canonical-json`, `frozen` and the four `python-*` standard-library ports (D-0018) -- appearing in the five per-module functions; they are boundary cases with no source case because the modules themselves were created by the port. The last is the detector's `require(...)` and `import x = require(...)` routes: `tsc` refuses both in an ESM module under D-0003, so no source case and no real module exercises them, and machinery nothing asserts is untested surface -- the rule `test/testkit/testkit.contract.test.ts` already records. The handling stays because the sweep should not depend on the module setting staying what it is today.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: The POSIX-only-anchor sweep matches a `baseDir` property in an object literal. An anchor passed positionally -- `layerDocument(layer, origin, "/srv/catalog", data)` -- is not matched.
inherited_limitations.why: The source has the same hole and in the same place: it matches `keyword.arg != "base_dir"`, so a positional third argument to `layer_document` escapes it too. Carried over rather than widened, because widening it is a change to what the case asserts and belongs in the belt that needs it. What is added instead is the non-vacuity assertion the source lacks, which is what would catch the sweep silently matching nothing at all.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: The scan reads specifiers, not resolved semantics. A module reached through a specifier built at runtime -- `import(someVariable)` -- is invisible to it.
inherited_limitations.why: The source has the identical limitation for the identical reason: `ast.Import` carries a name, not a computed value, so `importlib.import_module(name)` is invisible there too. Closing it requires resolving arbitrary expressions, which is a type checker's job and not a boundary check's. Neither tree contains such a call today.
